reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces, most often due to obstruction of urinary outflow but sometimes non-obstructive, and it is a radiological finding rather than a diagnosis in itself
The clinical priority is to determine whether true obstruction is present, since obstruction threatens renal function, whereas dilatation without obstruction may need only surveillance
Causes are classified by level: intraluminal (stones, clots, tumour), mural (pelviureteric junction obstruction, strictures), and extrinsic (pelvic masses, retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy)
Acute unilateral obstruction typically causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain, whereas chronic or bilateral obstruction may be insidious with vague symptoms or present with renal impairment
Obstruction combined with infection above the blockage produces an infected, obstructed system (pyonephrosis), a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage and antibiotics
Bilateral hydronephrosis or hydronephrosis of a solitary kidney can cause acute kidney injury and post-obstructive changes, and demands prompt relief
Antenatally detected hydronephrosis is common and often transient, but significant or persistent dilatation needs postnatal assessment for underlying uropathy and reflux
Ultrasound is the first-line investigation, with CT and functional renography used to define the cause, level, and the affected kidney's function and drainage
Relief of obstruction is achieved by drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) followed by treatment directed at the underlying cause
reference.pathophysiology: When urine outflow is obstructed, pressure builds up proximal to the blockage and is transmitted back to the renal pelvis and calyces, causing them to dilate. Persistently raised intrapelvic and intratubular pressure impairs glomerular filtration and, over time, produces progressive tubular and parenchymal damage with cortical thinning and loss of function. Superimposed infection in a stagnant, obstructed system allows rapid bacterial proliferation and pus accumulation. Non-obstructive hydronephrosis arises where the collecting system is dilated without a pressure gradient, for example vesicoureteric reflux, high urine flow, or a capacious but unobstructed system, and these generally do not damage the kidney.
additionalDifferentials: Extrinsic compression by pelvic or retroperitoneal masses, or retroperitoneal fibrosis
Extrarenal pelvis or parapelvic cyst mimicking dilatation
additionalInvestigations: Renal tract ultrasound as first-line to confirm and grade dilatation
CT urography or non-contrast CT to identify stones, level, and cause of obstruction
Diuretic renography (e.g. MAG3) to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive dilatation and assess differential function
Serum creatinine and electrolytes to assess renal function
Urinalysis and culture to detect infection
Micturating cystourethrogram in children where reflux is suspected
redFlags: Infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) with fever, loin pain, and sepsis requiring emergency drainage
Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney causing acute kidney injury
Anuria or rapidly rising creatinine indicating significant obstructive nephropathy
Severe uncontrolled pain or haemodynamic instability
Post-obstructive diuresis after relief, risking fluid and electrolyte disturbance
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause, the duration and completeness of obstruction, and whether infection intervenes. Prompt relief of acute obstruction usually allows recovery of renal function, but prolonged or severe obstruction leads to irreversible parenchymal loss. Non-obstructive dilatation and much antenatally detected hydronephrosis resolve or remain stable without harm. Infected obstruction is life-threatening if drainage is delayed but recovers well with timely intervention.
pitfalls: Assuming all dilatation means obstruction and intervening unnecessarily
Failing to recognise and urgently drain an infected obstructed system
Overlooking bladder outlet obstruction as a cause of bilateral upper tract dilatation
Not anticipating and managing post-obstructive diuresis after relieving obstruction
Delaying functional imaging so that salvageable renal function is lost
management: Urgent decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent for obstruction complicated by acute kidney injury, infection, or a solitary kidney
Emergency drainage combined with antibiotics for an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis)
Definitive treatment of the underlying cause, such as stone removal, pyeloplasty for pelviureteric junction obstruction, or relief of bladder outlet obstruction
Monitoring of renal function and anticipation of post-obstructive diuresis after relief of obstruction
Surveillance rather than intervention for non-obstructive dilatation confirmed on diuretic renography
Investigation and management of reflux in children, with micturating cystourethrography where indicated
Urological multidisciplinary follow-up to preserve renal function
